title: Satyakama comes home to his teacher
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hookLine: Satyakama learns from a bull, a fire, a swan and a diving bird, and still goes home to his teacher
carry: knowledge from a teacher reaches its goal
tomorrow: what if the rule book has no rule for this?
last: THE HEART IS A ROOT OF DHARMA.

lines: A BULL, A FIRE, A SWAN, A DIVING BIRD.
cards: Remember Satyakama, the boy who told the truth at the door? His teacher gave him four hundred thin, weak cows. Satyakama said: I won't come back until they're a thousand.
He was gone for years. When the herd reached a thousand, the bull spoke to him and taught him a part of Brahman, the reality in everything. Then the fire taught him a part.
Then a swan. Then a diving bird. He walked home glowing, and his teacher saw it the moment he arrived.

teach.h: YOU SHINE LIKE ONE WHO KNOWS BRAHMAN.
teach.b: Gautama said, in paraphrase: you shine like one who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Others than people, said Satyakama.
But teach me yourself, sir. I've heard that knowledge learned from a teacher reaches its goal. And the teacher taught him the same, leaving nothing out.
That's the teaching under this whole week, and the honest answer to 'so you just pick and choose?' In this tradition you don't weigh alone.

The week turned up the tools: a story kept; smriti giving way to the Veda; the dharma of an age, argued by Vidyasagar and his opponents; a handful of rice kept daily; Ambedkar's refusal; and the heart, last of Manu's four roots.
Even Satyakama, who'd learned from a bull and the fire, took it back to a teacher.
Picking at random needs none of that. Weighing needs the texts, a teacher, and a heart shaped by both. One question is still open: when the book itself has no rule at all, who decides?

how: Hindu teachers and reformers have weighed the dharma books with the tradition's own tools: the Veda above smriti, the dharma of an age, the conduct of the good and conscience; and many Hindus still learn the texts from a teacher rather than alone.

games.q: what does “with the keeper's framing of what” mean?
o: what a tradition weighs, keeps and sets down
the punishments listed in an old law book
the order in which a home rite is performed

games.q: the week's tools — tap the pairs.

s: Satyakama learned from the bull and the fire, so he no longer needed a teacher
he asked Gautama to teach him anyway: knowledge from a teacher reaches its goal.
the Manusmriti itself says it is remembered, not heard
its second chapter: shruti is the Veda, smriti the dharma books.

games.q: you've worked something out about dharma on your own, and it feels right. what would Satyakama do next?
o: take it to a teacher and ask them to teach it too.
post it; if it feels right, it is right.
keep it to myself; nobody else needs to check it.
games.why: he'd learned from a bull, the fire, a swan and a diving bird, and still asked Gautama: knowledge from a teacher reaches its goal.

practice: If you pray, bow your head for your teachers, the people who handed things on to you, the way Satyakama came home to his. If you don't pray, bring one teacher to mind and thank them silently.
Then rest with the breath until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Kept and rejected: what a tradition holds on to and what it lets go, weighed with its own tools and a teacher, not alone.

orig.note: Sanskrit acharya, teacher: Satyakama says knowledge learned from a teacher reaches its goal (Chandogya 4.9).

carryVoice: Hold this close: knowledge from a teacher reaches its goal. Satyakama, glowing, still came home to ask. That's the week.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.5–4.9 (Satyakama tends the cows until they are a thousand; the bull, the fire, a swan and a diving bird each teach him a quarter of Brahman; Gautama: you shine like one who knows Brahman; knowledge learned from a teacher reaches its goal)
